edges.description: Without C2 there is no C4b2a, so the classical pathway cannot generate C3 convertase activity.
edges.source: C2 Gene Defect and Absent C2 Protein

edges.description: Failure to deposit C3b on encapsulated organisms impairs opsonophagocytic clearance.
Classical pathway activity is required to solubilise immune complexes and clear apoptotic cells; its loss permits their persistence.
edges.target: Defective Immune Complex and Apoptotic Debris Clearance

edges.description: Failure of opsonophagocytic clearance manifests as recurrent invasive pyogenic infection.
Persisting apoptotic debris is a sustained source of nuclear autoantigen.
edges.source: Defective Immune Complex and Apoptotic Debris Clearance
edges.target: Loss of Tolerance to Nuclear Autoantigen

edges.description: Loss of tolerance manifests as clinical systemic lupus erythematosus in roughly a quarter of individuals with complete C2 deficiency.
edges.source: Loss of Tolerance to Nuclear Autoantigen

nodes.description: The predominant type I allele carries a 28-bp deletion at the exon 6 exon/intron boundary, introducing an early stop codon so that no C2 protein reaches plasma. Type II alleles instead permit synthesis but block secretion.
nodes.id: C2 Gene Defect and Absent C2 Protein

evidence.reference_title: Strong Association of Combined Genetic Deficiencies in the Classical Complement Pathway With Risk of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Primary Sjogren's Syndrome.
evidence.snippet: The predominant cause of complete C2 deficiency is a 28‐bp deletion (rs9332736) in the exon/intron boundary of exon 6.

evidence.reference_title: A novel type II complement C2 deficiency allele in an African-American family.
evidence.snippet: Pulse-chase biosynthetic labeling experiments indicated that the C111Y mutant C2 was retained by transfected COS cells and secreted only in minimal amounts.

nodes.description: C2 is an obligate component of the classical pathway C3 convertase C4b2a. Its absence blocks classical-pathway C3 cleavage, measurable as absent CH50. The alternative and lectin pathways remain intact, which is why the phenotype is milder than a C3 deficiency.

evidence.reference_title: Strong Association of Combined Genetic Deficiencies in the Classical Complement Pathway With Risk of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Primary Sjogren's Syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Reduced C2 levels in plasma (P = 2 × 10-9 ) and impaired function of the classical complement pathway (P = 0.03) were detected in SLE patients with heterozygous C2 deficiency.

nodes.description: Classical-pathway activity is required to solubilise immune complexes and to opsonise apoptotic cells for silent clearance. Without it, both persist.
nodes.id: Defective Immune Complex and Apoptotic Debris Clearance

evidence.reference_title: Strong Association of Combined Genetic Deficiencies in the Classical Complement Pathway With Risk of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Primary Sjogren's Syndrome.
evidence.snippet: In contrast, complete C2 deficiency is one of the most common complement deficiencies, with an estimated prevalence of 1:20,000 in the Swedish population and a penetrance for SLE of ~25%

nodes.description: Without classical-pathway C3b deposition on encapsulated organisms, chiefly Streptococcus pneumoniae, phagocytes cannot engage them efficiently through complement receptors.

evidence.reference_title: Immunoglobulin deficiencies and susceptibility to infection among homozygotes and heterozygotes for C2 deficiency.
evidence.snippet: About 25% of C2-deficient homozygotes have increased susceptibility to severe bacterial infections.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical and Genetic Spectrum of a Large Cohort With Total and Sub-total Complement Deficiencies.
evidence.snippet: Our study confirms the strong association of meningococcal infections with terminal pathway deficiency and highlights the risk of pneumococcal and auto-immune diseases in the classical and alternative pathways.

nodes.description: Sustained exposure to uncleared nuclear autoantigen drives loss of B- and T-cell tolerance and anti-nuclear autoantibody production. This is the accepted explanation for the SLE association, but the step from impaired clearance to autoantibody production has not been demonstrated directly in C2-deficient patients — see the knowledge gap below.
nodes.id: Loss of Tolerance to Nuclear Autoantigen
